chapter_theme: Kindly regard is what eyes are for and what keeps the world's dealings going; eyes without it are wounds or dead wood. Yet the chapter also sets a limit on it, that it must not undo one's duty, and then praises enduring poison for its sake.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: its excellence (571-572), the fault of the eye that does not extend it (573-575), the low standing of those who withhold it (576-577), how to extend it (578), and its proper scope, namely wrongs done to oneself (579-580).

571.reading: Because that surpassingly great beauty called kindly regard exists, this world exists.
571.nuance: A word of ornament (காரிகை) is given the weight of a cosmic condition. The chapter's elevated claim starts by calling kindness a beauty, not a duty.

positions.position: The beauty is the king's, and without it his subjects live like deer beside a tiger.
positions.quote: கண்ணோட்டம் என்று சொல்லப்படுகின்ற சிறப்பு உடைய அழகு அரசர்மாட்டு உண்டு ஆகலான்

positions.position: The verse is about anyone who has this quality, and they bring the world its greatness.
positions.quote: பெரும் அழகைக் கொண்டவர்கள் இருப்பதால்தான் பெருமை அடைகிறது.

572.reading: The world's ordinary workings rest on kindly regard, and the mere existence of those without it is a weight on the earth.
572.nuance: Parimelazhagar lists what உலகியல் consists of: mutual helpfulness, protection, and forgiving lapses. On that reading the grace of the eye is social infrastructure, not private sentiment.

573.reading: Of what use is melody that does not fit the song? Of what use is an eye with no kindly regard?
573.nuance: The analogy treats kindness as attunement: the eye is related to regard as melody is related to singing, so it needs the other to fulfil itself. Parimelazhagar's long list of musical terms is a resource for the music tradition more than for the verse's argument.

574.reading: What do eyes that lack measured kindly regard do, beyond seeming to be there in the face?
574.nuance: அளவினால் is easy to skip: even while condemning the lack, the verse measures the virtue, and Parimelazhagar takes this as excluding excess of it. This prepares for 578.

575.reading: Kindly regard is the eye's only jewel, and without it the eye is known for a wound.
575.nuance: The wound is what the observer perceives (உணரப் படும்), so the verse judges the eye by how it meets others.

576.reading: Those who have eyes yet do not turn them kindly on others are like trees fixed in the soil.

positions.position: It means a real tree, which stands joined to earth: they walk about but are as unresponsive as trees. He rejects the plaster-puppet reading.
positions.quote: அதனைச் சுதைமண்ணோடு கூடிய மரப்பாவை என்று உரைப்பாரும் உளர். அஃது உரையன்மை

positions.position: It means a wooden doll made with plaster: people whose eyes have met another's and still show no regard are like the doll.

577.reading: Those without kindly regard have no eyes, and those who truly have eyes do not lack it.
577.nuance: The verse redefines possession of eyes by function. The second half turns the first around, closing off the idea of a sighted person who merely chooses not to look kindly.

578.reading: The world belongs to those able to extend kindly regard without damaging the task at hand.
578.nuance: வல்லார் marks this as a skill and a difficult one. After seven verses of unqualified praise, the condition here gives the whole chapter its hard edge.

positions.position: The task is the king's justice, which fails if he spares associates who have harmed others.
positions.quote: முறை செய்தல் ஆகிய தன் தொழில் அழியாமல்

positions.position: The task is the king's own interests: kindness must not cost him material loss.
positions.quote: அரசர்க்குப் பொருட்கேடு வாராமல் கண்ணோட வேண்டுமென்று கூறிற்று.

579.reading: The highest disposition is to extend kindly regard and bear with even those whose way is to hurt you.

positions.position: பண்பினார் implies familiarity: those meant are people close to the king, and this is the top quality in kings.
It extends to anyone at all who is inclined to destroy you.

580.reading: Those who want a refinement worth loving will see poison poured, drink it, and stay at ease.
580.nuance: The verse names no pourer: the 'friends' in Pope and the associates in Parimelazhagar are supplied. Parimelazhagar's support comes from Natrinai 355, which offers a thread beyond the Kural, and it is where the identification of நாகரிகம with kindly regard rests.

positions.position: நாகரிகம is kindly regard, and the poison comes from associates whom one's eyes cannot refuse.
நாகரிகம is the broader possession of good qualities across virtue, wealth and pleasure.
positions.quote: நாகரிகம் - அறம் பொருள் இன்பத்தின்கண் நற்குணங்கள் பலவும் உடைமை

links.note: 541 defines justice partly as not extending கண்ணோட்டம் (ஓர்ந்துகண் ணோடாது). This chapter says the world depends on it. 578 is the hinge, and Parimelazhagar cites 541 there: the same grace is the condition of the world and a corruption of justice, depending on where it falls.

578 forbids kindness that damages the work, and 580 praises kindness that swallows poison. Parimelazhagar resolves this by confining forbearance to wrongs against oneself, but the verses themselves don't state that limit.

Adjacent chapters use the same phrase, நிலக்குப் பொறை, for two different faults: the alliance of harshness with ignorance, and the mere lack of kindly regard. The second is far milder and yet receives the same verdict.
Both call failed eyes wounds. In 393 the eye is failed by lack of learning, and in 575 by lack of kindly regard. Taken together, an eye must both know and regard, and neither alone saves it.

If Manakkudavar's reading of 576 is right, both verses use the wooden doll for a person hollow inside: 1020 lacks shame and 576 lacks regard. On Parimelazhagar's reading the image is a rooted tree, and this parallel fades.

807 says those of long affection don't give it up even when ruined by friends. 580 gives the same stance its most extreme image. If Parimelazhagar is right that the poisoner is an associate, the poison verse belongs to the same ethic as the chapter on old friendship.

source_issues: 573: Manakkudavar's commentary is marked as not aligned in the source.
576: Manakkudavar's text reads மாப்பாவை where his closing line has மரப்பாவை, which looks like a text error.
